name: Sugar
description: Standard caloric sucrose derived from sugar cane or sugar beet.
common_uses: Sweetener, preservative, bulking agent in confectionery and beverages.
explanation: High intake of added sugars is linked to metabolic conditions, dental decay, and blood glucose spikes.

name: High Fructose Corn Syrup
description: Enzymatically processed corn syrup with high unbound fructose concentration.
common_uses: Soft drinks, sweetened juices, baked goods, sauces.
explanation: Rapidly absorbed fructose bypasses insulin signaling in the liver; linked to fatty liver, insulin resistance, and visceral adiposity.

name: Refined Wheat Flour
description: Endosperm of wheat milled after bran and germ removal.
common_uses: Bread, biscuits, noodles, pasta, pastries.
explanation: Stripped of dietary fibre and micronutrients; high glycemic index that prompts rapid insulin release.

name: Whole Wheat Flour
description: Intact grain flour retaining bran, germ, and starchy endosperm.
common_uses: Rotis, whole wheat breads, wholesome baked goods.
explanation: Contains natural fiber, B-vitamins, and minerals with steady glucose release.

name: Palm Oil
description: Tropical plant oil extracted from the pulp of oil palms.
common_uses: Frying fat, biscuit shortening, processed snacks, confectionery.
explanation: Contains ~50% saturated palmitic acid; high consumption raises LDL cholesterol and has notable environmental concerns.

name: Partially Hydrogenated Vegetable Oil
description: Industrially produced trans-fatty acids created through partial catalytic hydrogenation.
common_uses: Commercial bakery goods, fried packaged snacks, frosting.
explanation: Major source of artificial trans fats, which significantly raise LDL (bad) cholesterol and lower HDL (good) cholesterol, dramatically increasing cardiovascular disease risk.

name: Soy Lecithin
description: Phospholipid mixture extracted from soybeans that prevents separation of oil and water.
common_uses: Chocolates, bakery items, instant beverages, margarines.
explanation: Generally recognized as safe (GRAS); contains beneficial choline and phospholipids. Only caution is for individuals with severe soy allergy.

name: Citric Acid
description: Organic tricarboxylic acid widely found in citrus fruits or produced via Aspergillus niger fermentation.
common_uses: Acidulant, flavour enhancer, antioxidant booster in carbonated drinks, jams, and snacks.
explanation: Safe naturally occurring compound that participates in the Krebs cellular cycle.

name: Ascorbic Acid
description: Essential water-soluble antioxidant and nutrient.
common_uses: Flour treatment agent, preventing fruit browning, nutrient fortification.
explanation: Essential vitamin and powerful antioxidant protecting food against oxidative rancidity.
source_ref: EFSA Scientific Opinion on Vitamin C

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
description: Mineral salt that releases carbon dioxide when reacted with acid or heat.
common_uses: Leavening agent in cakes, cookies, and effervescent beverages.
explanation: Harmless mineral leavening agent with a long history of safe food usage.

name: Tartrazine
description: Synthetic azo dye providing bright lemon yellow coloration.
common_uses: Soft drinks, candy, packaged snacks, ice creams, processed sauces.
explanation: Southampton study linked azo dyes with hyperactivity in children; potential trigger for urticaria and asthma in sensitive or aspirin-intolerant individuals.
source_ref: Lancet Southampton Study / UK FSA Warning

name: Sunset Yellow FCF
description: Petroleum-derived synthetic azo dye yielding vivid orange hues.
common_uses: Snack chips, instant noodles, confectioneries, powdered drinks.
explanation: Synthetic dye associated with behavioural changes and hyperactivity in children, requiring warning labels in the European Union.

name: Titanium Dioxide
description: Inorganic mineral pigment used as an opaque white colouring and brightening agent.
common_uses: Candies, chewing gum, coffee whiteners, cake icings.
explanation: Banned in the European Union as a food additive due to concerns regarding nanoparticle accumulation and potential genotoxicity.

name: Caramel IV
description: Heat-treated carbohydrate colorant prepared in the presence of sulphite and ammonium compounds.
common_uses: Colas, dark beers, gravy browning, baked goods, sauces.
explanation: Manufacturing by-product 4-MEI (4-methylimidazole) is classified as a possible human carcinogen by IARC if consumed in excessive quantities.

name: Monosodium Glutamate
description: Sodium salt of glutamic acid producing pronounced umami/savoury sensation.
common_uses: Instant noodles, savory crisps, frozen meals, Chinese cuisine, soups.
explanation: Safe for the general population according to FDA/EFSA, but may provoke transient headache, flushing, or numbness in sensitive individuals.
source_ref: US FDA Food Additive Review on Glutamates

name: Disodium Inosinate
description: Nucleotide flavour enhancer that works synergistically with MSG.
common_uses: Seasoning blends, chips, instant noodles, processed snacks.
allergen_info: May be derived from fish or meat
explanation: Frequently prepared from animal or fish sources (such as sardines or meat extracts); vegetarians and vegans should verify source origin with the manufacturer.

name: Sodium Benzoate
description: Sodium salt of benzoic acid functioning as an antimicrobial against yeasts and moulds in acidic media.
common_uses: Soft drinks, pickles, salad dressings, fruit juices.
explanation: When combined with ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) in acidic conditions and exposed to light or heat, can form trace benzene (a known carcinogen).
source_ref: FDA Survey of Benzene in Soft Drinks

name: Potassium Sorbate
description: Polyunsaturated fatty acid salt inhibiting mold and yeast development.
common_uses: Cheese, yogurt, baked goods, wine, dried fruits, syrups.
explanation: Metabolized by the human body like dietary fatty acids into carbon dioxide and water.
source_ref: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources

name: BHA (Butylated Hydroxyanisole)
description: Synthetic phenolic antioxidant added to fats to prevent lipid oxidation and rancidity.
common_uses: Chips, butter, lard, dehydrated meat, chewing gum.
explanation: Anticipated human carcinogen according to the US National Toxicology Program; banned or restricted in several European jurisdictions.

name: BHT (Butylated Hydroxytoluene)
description: Synthetic lipophilic organic compound preventing fat spoilage.
common_uses: Breakfast cereals, snack foods, chewing gum, shortening.
explanation: Synthetic antioxidant with disputed endocrine disrupting potential in animal models; some consumer groups recommend avoidance.

name: Sodium Metabisulphite
description: Inorganic sulfur compound acting as a sanitizer, antioxidant, and preservative.
common_uses: Dried fruits, wines, vinegar, biscuits, potato chips.
explanation: Releases sulphur dioxide which can trigger acute respiratory bronchospasms and anaphylactoid reactions in asthmatics.

name: Aspartame
description: Low-calorie artificial dipeptide sweetener roughly 200 times sweeter than table sugar.
common_uses: Diet sodas, sugar-free chewing gum, low-calorie desserts.
explanation: Classified by WHO/IARC in 2023 as 'possibly carcinogenic to humans' (Group 2B); strictly contraindicated for individuals with phenylketonuria (PKU).

name: Sucralose
description: Non-nutritive chlorinated carbohydrate sweetener ~600 times sweeter than sucrose.
common_uses: Sugar-free syrups, baked goods, protein powders, diet soft drinks.
explanation: Emerging studies suggest potential alterations to gut microbiome balance and insulin sensitivity when heated or consumed long term.

name: Acesulfame Potassium
description: Calorie-free sweetener often combined with aspartame or sucralose to mask bitter aftertastes.
common_uses: Diet drinks, protein shakes, sugar-free confectioneries.
explanation: Synthetic sweetener containing methylene chloride breakdown impurities; animal studies warrant moderate caution.
source_ref: Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI)

name: Carrageenan
description: Sulphated polysaccharide extracted from edible red seaweeds.
common_uses: Dairy alternatives, almond milk, deli meats, ice creams.
explanation: Degraded forms (poligeenan) can trigger intestinal inflammation, ulceration, and gastrointestinal distress in sensitive guts.

name: Mono- and Diglycerides of Fatty Acids
description: Synthetic or semi-synthetic fat emulsifiers composed of glycerol bound to one or two fatty acids.
common_uses: Bread, ice cream, margarine, packaged cake mixes, peanut butter.
explanation: Can be derived from either vegetable oils or animal fats (bovine/swine tallow). Origin must be confirmed for vegetarian, vegan, and halal compliance.

name: Gelatin
description: Water-soluble protein extracted by boiling animal skins, bones, and connective tissue.
common_uses: Gummy candies, marshmallows, jelly cups, capsule coatings, yogurt.
explanation: Directly derived from animal slaughter byproduct (pig skin, cow hides, bones). Strictly non-vegetarian and non-vegan.

name: Carmine
description: Deep red pigment produced by crushing dried female cochineal insects (Dactylopius coccus).
common_uses: Strawberry yogurts, fruit juices, candies, cosmetics, maraschino cherries.
explanation: Derived from crushed insects. Not suitable for vegetarians or vegans, and known to induce allergic reactions or contact urticaria.
source_ref: FDA Labeling Requirements for Cochineal Extract

name: Milk Solids
description: Dehydrated residue of milk containing proteins, lactose, and minerals.
common_uses: Chocolate, cookies, breads, protein shakes, ice creams.
explanation: Wholesome dairy nutrient source; unsuitable for vegans and persons with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

name: Peanuts
description: Legume seed high in protein and monounsaturated fatty acids.
common_uses: Peanut butter, energy bars, baked goods, Asian curries, snacks.
explanation: Nutritious whole food, but one of the most severe food allergens capable of triggering fatal anaphylactic shock in sensitized individuals.

name: Xanthan Gum
description: Polysaccharide fermented by Xanthomonas campestris bacterium using glucose or sucrose.
common_uses: Salad dressings, gluten-free baking, sauces, ice cream.
explanation: Safe soluble dietary fiber with zero toxicity. Provides texture without added caloric fats.

name: Maltodextrin
description: Hydrolyzed starch polymer providing mild sweetness and bulking volume.
common_uses: Seasoning carrier, chips powder, sports supplements, infant formulas.
allergen_info: May contain trace Wheat if wheat-derived
explanation: Has a very high glycemic index (GI 110-185), causing higher blood sugar spikes than pure table sugar.
